games.title: Civilization (board game)
games.note: Francis Tresham's board game of ancient civilizations; Avalon Hill later licensed the name to MicroProse.

games.title: 1830: The Game of Railroads and Robber Barons
games.note: Railway-building and stock-trading board game, developed from Tresham's earlier 1829.

games.title: Railroad Tycoon
games.note: Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley's railway empire game: lay track, run trains and fight rival barons on the stock market.

games.title: Civilization III
games.note: Added national borders drawn by culture, and strategic resources such as iron and oil.

games.title: Civilization VII
games.note: Released February 2025. Each campaign runs through three ages, and you can switch to a new civilization at each one.

games.title: Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri
games.note: Brian Reynolds led the design: ideological factions colonize an alien planet whose native life fights back.

games.title: Stellar Conquest
games.note: A board game of exploring and colonizing star systems, later named as an influence on early 4X computer games.

games.title: Reach for the Stars
games.dev: Strategic Studies Group (Roger Keating, Ian Trout)
games.note: An Australian space strategy game that tied economic growth, research and conquest together.

games.title: Master of Orion
games.note: Alan Emrich's preview of it in Computer Gaming World coined the term '4X': explore, expand, exploit, exterminate.

games.title: Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares
Master of Magic
games.note: Rival wizards research spells and raise armies across two linked worlds, Arcanus and Myrror.

games.title: Galactic Civilizations
games.note: A Windows remake of Stardock's own 1990s OS/2 game, known for its strong computer opponents.

games.title: Endless Space
games.note: The first game from Amplitude, a Paris studio founded in 2011.

games.title: Humankind
games.note: In each era you adopt a new culture, so your nation's history becomes a blend of peoples.

games.title: Stellaris
games.note: Paradox's space strategy game, with generated galaxies, alien empires, late-game crises and buildable Dyson spheres.

games.title: Europa Universalis (board game)
games.note: Philippe Thibaut's board game of early modern European empires, the basis of Paradox's first grand strategy game.

games.title: Europa Universalis
games.note: Paradox's first grand strategy game, played on a real-time map of the world from 1492 that you can pause.

games.title: Hearts of Iron
games.note: Paradox's grand strategy game of the Second World War.

games.title: Victoria: An Empire Under the Sun
games.note: Paradox's grand strategy game of the 19th century, focused on economies, politics and population groups.

games.title: Crusader Kings
games.note: Paradox's medieval grand strategy game, where you play a dynasty rather than a country.

games.title: Crusader Kings II
games.note: When your ruler dies you carry on as the heir, so plotting, marriages and murders drive the stories.

games.title: Total War: Warhammer
games.note: Creative Assembly's first fantasy Total War, with monsters, flying units and magic.

games.title: King's Bounty
games.note: Recruit an army, hunt down villains and find the Sceptre of Order before time runs out.

games.title: Songs of Conquest
games.note: A Swedish pixel-art fantasy strategy game whose armies are led by spellcasting Wielders. Early access from 2022.

games.title: M.U.L.E.
games.note: Four players settle a planet and trade at live auctions. Will Wright later dedicated The Sims to Bunten's memory.

games.title: Pikmin
games.note: Shigeru Miyamoto's game of directing up to a hundred plant creatures to carry, build and fight.

links.took: Many technology tree ideas, and the idea of a whole civilization's rise as a game.
links.added: A world map, cities, wonders and history running all the way to space flight.
links.extra: Meier has said the board game influenced his design far less than the computer game Empire did.

links.took: An open-ended 'god game' you play as a guiding hand rather than a character.
links.added: A whole world, rival civilizations, war, diplomacy and a tech tree.
links.extra: Meier set out to try new kinds of games after SimCity and Populous succeeded.

links.took: The god game: guiding a whole people from above.
links.added: Thousands of years of history, cities you manage and turn-based play.

links.took: Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley's partnership and their growing, interlocking economic systems.
links.added: Turned from railways to the whole of human history.
links.extra: Same two designers, one year apart.

links.took: Railway building mixed with share trading and hostile takeovers.
links.added: Real-time trains, freight that responds to supply and demand, and a computer that runs the economy.
links.extra: Wikipedia calls 1830 the original idea and inspiration; Meier credited Tresham's design.

links.took: Track laying, train scheduling and stock-market battles.
links.added: Higher-resolution maps, scenarios across eras and more detailed finance.
links.extra: Developed by PopTop Software rather than MicroProse.

links.took: Building a profitable rail network that carries goods and passengers between towns.
links.added: An isometric view and roads, ships and aircraft alongside trains.

src.t: Chris Sawyer, quoted in The Digital Antiquarian, 2020

links.extra: Sawyer: 'I was fascinated with Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon game.'

links.took: Turn-based empire building, the tech tree, wonders and city management.
links.added: Culture that pushes out national borders, strategic resources and trade.

links.took: Cultural borders and strategic resources.
links.added: Religions, Great People and full 3D graphics.

links.took: Hex maps, districts and turn-based history from antiquity onward.
links.added: Three ages per campaign, separate leaders and civilizations, and switching civilization between ages.
links.extra: The age-by-age civilization swap divided players; a 2026 update lets you keep one civilization.

links.took: Brian Reynolds and Sid Meier's Civilization formula of cities, research and diplomacy.
links.added: A science-fiction story on an alien planet, ideological factions and units you design yourself.
links.extra: Reynolds and Meier left MicroProse to found Firaxis.

links.took: Colonizing an alien world with factions and a hostile native ecosystem.
links.added: Affinities that steer your colony toward harmony, purity or supremacy.
links.extra: Wikipedia calls it a spiritual sequel to Alpha Centauri; both are by Firaxis.

links.took: Exploring and colonizing star systems while building fleets against rivals.
links.added: A computer to run the economy and research, and computer-controlled opponents.
links.extra: Wikipedia says early 4X games were influenced by board games such as Stellar Conquest.

links.took: The link between economic growth, research and conquest across a galaxy.
links.added: Distinct alien races, ship design, diplomacy and a much deeper tech tree.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Master of Orion drew on earlier 4X games such as Reach for the Stars.

links.took: The turn-based empire game of exploring, expanding and researching that Civilization popularized.
links.added: Moved it to a galaxy of star systems with custom warships.

links.took: Galactic 4X play with distinct races, research and ship design.
links.added: Custom races, hero leaders, tactical space combat and the Antarans.

src.t: Wikipedia: Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares

links.took: SimTex and Steve Barcia's 4X design.
links.added: A fantasy setting, wizards casting spells, and heroes leading armies.
links.extra: Same studio and designer.

links.took: The city-founding, research-driven empire game Civilization popularized.
links.added: Magic research instead of technology, and tactical battles with monsters.

links.took: Turn-based galactic empire building with alien races and ship design.
links.added: Strong computer opponents and an ethical alignment system for your civilization.
links.extra: Wikipedia notes the 2003 release was compared favorably with Master of Orion.

links.took: The space 4X formula that Master of Orion II made a genre standard.
links.added: Simultaneous turns, card-based space battles and a slick, modern interface.

links.took: Amplitude's Endless universe and 4X design.
links.added: A fantasy planet with very different factions and seasons, including harsh winters.

links.took: Amplitude's 4X systems and hex-based regions.
links.added: Real history, where you adopt a new culture each era.
links.extra: Same studio.

links.took: The historical 4X that Civilization popularized: from first cities to the modern age.
links.added: Mixing cultures across eras and winning on fame rather than a single victory type.

links.took: Galactic 4X play with alien species, research and fleets.
links.added: Paradox's pausable real time, crises late in the game and deep species customization.

links.took: Paradox's grand strategy engine and its emergent, event-driven stories.
links.added: A generated galaxy, alien species and space exploration.
links.extra: Same studio and engine.

links.took: The board game's map of early modern Europe, its nations and its historical scope.
links.added: Pausable real time, computer opponents and the whole world to colonize.
links.extra: An official adaptation of Philippe Thibaut's board game.

links.took: Nations from the age of discovery on a pausable world map.
links.added: Monarch points, trade networks and decades of expansions.

links.took: Paradox's pausable world map, provinces and nation-scale strategy.
links.added: The Second World War, with divisions, production and air and naval war.
links.extra: Built by the same studio on the same engine.

links.took: Grand strategy of the Second World War.
links.added: Drawing battle plans with arrows, focus trees and division designer.

links.took: Paradox's pausable world map and nation-scale strategy.
links.added: The 19th century, with industry, markets and populations that vote and revolt.

src.t: Wikipedia: Victoria: An Empire Under the Sun

links.took: The 19th-century focus on economics, politics and population groups.
links.added: A building-based economy and interest groups shaping laws.

links.took: Paradox's pausable map strategy and historical scope.
links.added: Playing a family dynasty, with characters, marriages and inheritance.

links.took: Dynasty-based medieval strategy.
links.added: Richer character traits, plots, factions and many expansions.

links.took: Dynasties, intrigue and inheritance in medieval Europe and beyond.
links.added: 3D character portraits, stress and lifestyles that shape your ruler.

links.took: The Total War mix of a turn-based campaign map and huge real-time battles.
links.added: Fantasy races with very different armies, flying monsters, heroes and spells.

links.took: The Old World setting, its races and their units from the tabletop game.
links.added: Total War's campaign map and battles with thousands of soldiers.
links.extra: An official adaptation.

links.took: A hero who recruits creature stacks, roams a map and fights turn-based battles.
links.added: Competing players, towns to build up and a turn-based strategy map.

src.t: Wikipedia: Heroes of Might and Magic: A Strategic Quest

links.extra: Both designed by Jon Van Caneghem at New World Computing.

links.took: The name and the hero-with-an-army adventure.
links.added: 3D world, rage-powered companions and a humorous story.

links.took: The hero-led army strategy that Heroes III made the genre's best-known form.
links.added: Pixel art, Wielders who cast spells from essence and a map editor.

links.took: Shigeru Miyamoto cited it as an influence.
links.added: Directing crowds of plant creatures in real time across a garden-like world.
links.extra: The source does not say which part of M.U.L.E. he meant.
